targets.oldText: Read the supplied enquiry title and source labels first. Place one approved factor card under long-term condition, short-term pressure or trigger, then quote no more than the necessary locator and paraphrase the relevant evidence. Build a cause chain using ‘made more likely’, ‘increased pressure’ or ‘triggered at this point’ only where the source supports that relationship. Add a counter-check: what would be missing if this factor were removed from the explanation? For the ethical decision, use the supplied fictional or historical classroom scenario rather than a learner's experience. Identify the decision-maker, available options, people affected and evidence limits. Compare one duty-based reason, one likely-consequence reason and one fairness or rights reason. Finish with a provisional judgement whose wording reflects uncertainty and does not label a person as simply good or bad. Produce a structured explanation of the supplied 20th-century conflict using the approved classroom pack. Select at least four causal factors, retain each source locator, classify the time scale, and explain two relationships between factors. Identify the factor presented as the immediate trigger and explain why a trigger is not the whole cause. Include one source limitation or contested interpretation that the pack identifies. Then complete an ethical decision matrix for the supplied scenario: options, relevant duties or rights, likely benefits and harms, who may be affected, uncertainty, and a reasoned provisional choice. Connect the two halves only at the level of reasoning—both require claims, evidence and limits. Do not make a present-day claim, invent an actor's motive, reconstruct a quotation, or turn an adult model into learner wording. The finished response may be spoken, signed, typed, diagrammed or exactly scribed. The named conflict, dates, actors and circumstances come only from the school-approved source pack; no missing fact is supplied from memory. Long-term conditions, short-term pressures and a trigger can interact, so a list becomes an explanation only when relationships are stated and evidenced. An ethical decision can compare duties, rights, likely consequences, fairness and uncertainty without pretending that every reasonable person reaches the same judgement. A source-supported explanation distinguishes what the evidence establishes, what is an interpretation and what remains uncertain. Sort supplied factors into long-term, short-term and trigger; complete two cause-and-evidence frames; then use prepared duty, harm and fairness cards to compare two options. Write a multi-cause explanation with source locators and linked factors, then compare ethical reasons and justify a provisional decision with one uncertainty. Evaluate the relative weight of competing causes, test a counterfactual carefully, compare ethical frameworks and defend a judgement while acknowledging a credible alternative and evidential limit.
